title: Two Difficult Tasks
hook: The best-feeling interview may be the weakest evidence you gather.
counterintuition: The hard part is not being decisive. It is showing which answer, act, or result the decision rests on before the cost moves later.
tryThisNow: Cross-out one broad interview question in 10 minutes; then write the job requirement beside one past-behavior ask and one job problem.
keyTakeaway: Define the demand before the hard talk. Interviews need past acts and job problems tied to the role; correction needs the gap, proof, change, and consequence.

breakdown.fastRead:
The best-feeling interview can be the weakest evidence when task-focused questions arrive too late. A short interview must predict later job performance from selected history, so each question has to pull past acts or job reasoning toward the actual task first. That is the miss.

When the job demand stays blank, the hiring lead asks for a broad self-story, likes the answer, and calls that smooth talk fit before task proof appears. The cost moves. The team pays with weaker output, extra help, and later correction. The repair is plain: put the role demand ahead of the question. Use past behavior examples and job-related problems, then compare the answer with the role.
breakdown.deepRead:
A question earns trust only after the role demand is known. It works because the answer now has a scale: the real role demand. Without that scale, charm fills the empty space. It may sound like proof. It is not.

Task-focused interview questions pull three things into view. They ask for past behavior examples, job-related problems, and requirements-based evidence. A task problem is not useful because it is hard. It is useful because the answer can be compared with actual task demands.

Write the demand before the question. If the role needs judgment under a real task, ask for a past act that shows that judgment or a job problem that lets the candidate reason through it. That is the split. The interview does not reveal fit; the requirement reveals which answers count. Smooth talk can help the exchange, but it cannot become the proof.

Daniel cannot state a missed standard and expect Grace to infer the behavior, the future target, and the stake in a serious correction talk alone. That gets a nod. It does not get repair. The line has to name the performance gap plus supporting evidence. Then it adds the stake.

When the evidence is missing, the hard line should wait, because a serious message without proof becomes pressure instead of a useful demand for change. Rank cannot fill it. If the role demand moved, reset the scale. If the line is serious, attach the consequence.
breakdown.fullRead:
The failure is easiest to see after the hire. The old screen has broad impressions, but no past examples, no job-related problems, and no requirements-based evidence tied to the role. The interview felt easy. It was thin.

Step one was the blank requirement. Evidence only has meaning against the task the person must do, so a general answer had no fair scale. What exactly was the person asked to prove? No one had written the specific job requirements before the question.

Step two was the broad self-description. The candidate could describe strengths, intent, and judgment without showing how they had acted. A hypothetical answer could sound careful without proving behavior. That was the trap.

Step three was the false prediction. A short interview window and selected history were all the interviewer had, so the call was always a bet about later job performance. Without task-focused questions, candidate evidence stayed thin and mood got too much weight. The team paid later through weaker output, more guidance, and correction effort.

Step four was the harder correction. Once the hire missed the task, authority could not explain which behavior or result created the concern. The person needed the performance gap, the supporting evidence, the expected change, and the consequence. Without those parts, the serious line could sound like ordinary advice.

The autopsy also shows why the repair feels slower. Task-focused questions narrow the talk, because the interviewer must give up the broad opener and use the role as the scale. That cost is real. It is still smaller than letting a weak prediction travel into the team.

Before the repair, a polished claim and a past act looked too much alike. After the repair, they split. Past examples showed what the person had done. Job-related problems showed how the person reasoned against the demand. Requirements-based evidence gave the yes or no a scale.

Evidence is the path from a claim to a visible act. In an interview, the path runs from role demand to candidate proof to task fit. In a correction talk, it runs from gap to proof to change and consequence. Which behavior created the concern? Which answer proved fit?

You can use the same discipline with no title power. Before asking a teammate for help, define the task and the proof you need. Before telling someone a promise slipped, cross out the trait label and name the act. The line gets shorter when the proof gets clearer.

This failed screen teaches one plain lesson. Do not trust the feeling of a hard talk until the evidence has done its job. Comfort can nod. Evidence can point.

examples.title: The Team Feels The Weak Question

planSpec.stakes: a weak screen moves cost into the team
planSpec.requiredBeat: the team feels the cost before the better question is named

examples.scenario: Outside the interview, the team first feels the weak screen. The candidate sounded strong, but the questions asked for broad self-description instead of past behavior examples or job-related problems tied to the requirement. The cost is extra guidance, weaker team output, and a correction later. The repair works only after the screen is rebuilt: before, claims; after, requirements-based evidence.
examples.whatToDo: What did skipping this cost? It moved the hiring bet into the team; replace the broad self-story with one past act and one role problem.
examples.whyItMatters: Why name the cost first? It keeps the better question earned: delay made the weak prediction expensive before anyone fixed the screen.

examples.title: The Late Task Problem

planSpec.requiredBeat: an early signal is caught just before mood takes over

examples.scenario: Nash sees the early signal: the missing requirement, but no one flags it. The missed-call screen glows while he keeps following the candidate's smooth self-description. The interview is headed for a mood-based yes and gets caught late, inside the short interview window. Before: liking and recency. After: job-related problems and requirements-based evidence.
examples.whatToDo: Why does the switch work? It restores the scale: ask a role problem, then compare the answer with the demand already written.
examples.whyItMatters: What made the catch late? Mood had almost outrun proof, so the short window left only one chance to turn back to evidence.

examples.title: Daniel Gets The Nod

planSpec.stakes: authority can win a nod and lose the change
planSpec.requiredBeat: a serious standard is stated without evidence

examples.scenario: "This standard has to change," lead Daniel says on a correction call. Grace asks, "Which behavior?" He answers from authority. He never names the performance gap, supporting evidence, or expected change and consequence. The miss lands before the talk ends. Grace hears dissatisfaction, not a serious target, so the later behavior has no clear line to meet.
examples.whatToDo: Which line is missing? State the act or result, the proof, the future target, and the consequence before rank enters.
examples.whyItMatters: Where does it fail? If proof is absent, authority only buys a nod; it cannot show Grace what to change.

examples.title: Grace Slows The Yes

planSpec.stakes: a fast yes can become a slow correction
planSpec.requiredBeat: the hiring demand is already past when the evidence is rebuilt

examples.scenario: Grace is crossing out the safe yes on a letter left on the table; the hiring demand is already past. The short interview window closed with selected history, not candidate evidence against the requirement. She rebuilds the call backward from the job demand. It works, but costs speed and comfort. Before: easy yes. After: task fit.
examples.whatToDo: Who decides now? Grace: restore the requirement, then decide from candidate evidence.
examples.whyItMatters: What changed? Comfort stopped carrying the call; task fit did.

questions.prompt: After Daniel gets a quiet nod in a correction talk, Grace still does not know what conduct caused the concern. Why did the talk fail?
choices: Daniel named the future target before Grace accepted the standard, so the line sounded like a demand fired by the wrong signal.
Daniel asked a senior title to back the message, so the judgment shifted away from the behavior Grace had to inspect.
Daniel leaned on authority without tying the concern to a concrete act or result Grace could understand.
questions.explanation: The key is the missing evidence. The senior-title choice is tempting, but borrowed force still would not tell Grace which behavior created the concern.

questions.prompt: Lacey has three possible interview prompts after the role demand is written, and the candidate will answer only one before time runs out. Which one should come first?
choices: Use a hard puzzle from another role, since the strain may reveal useful reasoning even if the task differs.
Use the prior panel's favorite puzzle, since a known prompt gives the interview a shared precedent.
Use a problem from the actual role, since the answer can be judged against the task itself.
questions.explanation: A role problem lets the interviewer compare reasoning with the real demand. A hard puzzle can impress, but it fails when difficulty outruns relevance.

questions.prompt: A hiring panel feels good about a candidate, then realizes it skipped its prepared task questions. What caused the bias?
choices: The panel let mood steer because requirements and preset questions were not holding attention on evidence.
The panel kept the exchange too short, so the candidate had little time to build rapport with the group.
The panel failed to let the highest-ranking interviewer decide first, so judgment spread across too many people.
questions.explanation: Preparation keeps attention on evidence rather than mood. More rapport would not fix the miss; it could make the same liking bias stronger.

questions.prompt: Grace states the performance gap and evidence in a serious correction talk, but Daniel hears the line as ordinary advice and treats it as optional. What was missing?
choices: A consequence that made the serious message carry stakes instead of sounding optional.
A softer close that kept Daniel from treating the message as punishment rather than guidance.
A second authority in the talk to show Daniel the concern had wider backing.
questions.explanation: The consequence makes the serious line real. A softer close may reduce strain, but it can also leave Daniel hearing a suggestion.

questions.prompt: Why did the warm interview still predict badly after the candidate's selected history sounded strong and the short screen felt easy?
choices: The candidate's old title carried more weight than any short exchange could correct during the screen.
The interviewer had to infer later job performance from a brief talk and selected history.
The conversation proved social ease, which was separate from the task the role required.
questions.explanation: An interview is a small prediction from limited material. Social ease may be real, but it does not prove future task performance.

questions.prompt: The team wants to accept a marginal hire and repair fit later. What should they expect?
choices: They should stop the search until every doubt disappears, because any later correction wastes effort.
The delay will push cost into team output, supervisory time, and later correction effort.
The risk will fall mostly on the candidate's confidence, while the team can absorb the task gap.
questions.explanation: Delay moves the cost downstream. Removing every doubt goes too far, but treating a weak fit as free ignores the later load.

questions.prompt: Before Nash writes the first interview question for a role he barely has time to screen, what belongs at the top of the page?
choices: The candidate's best story, so the exchange begins where the person feels strongest.
The job requirement, so each answer can be read against the task the person must do.
The panel's usual preference, so the call stays aligned with past hiring habit.
questions.explanation: The role demand gives evidence a scale. Letting the best story lead can sound fair, but it may miss task-specific fit.

questions.prompt: In a school project, Lacey tells a partner she is dissatisfied but the partner cannot tell what success would look like. Which response matches the same rule?
choices: Lacey should restate the dissatisfaction in stronger terms, since the feeling behind the concern was missed.
Lacey should cite only the past evidence, since naming a future target can make the request too rigid.
Lacey should name the exact change she wants, so the partner has a clear target for future behavior.
questions.explanation: The missing piece is the future target. Stronger dissatisfaction may sound clearer, but it still leaves the partner without a success line.

questions.prompt: Which candidate answer gives stronger evidence than abstract self-description when the interviewer needs behavior rather than a polished claim?
choices: A concrete example from past behavior that lets the interviewer inspect how the person acted.
A careful hypothetical about what the person would do if the same task appeared later.
A confident strengths summary that matches the interviewer's general feel for the role.
questions.explanation: Past behavior gives inspectable history. The hypothetical may be smart, but it can be prepared without showing what the person has done.

reviewCards.front: What comes before an interview question?
reviewCards.back: Define the job requirement first. Evidence only means something when it is read against the task the person must do.

reviewCards.front: Why ask for past behavior instead of self-description?
reviewCards.back: A past behavior example lets you inspect how the person acted. Self-description can sound strong without proving behavior.

reviewCards.front: When does a job problem help an interview?
reviewCards.back: It helps when the problem maps to the role. Then the answer can be compared with actual task demands.

reviewCards.front: What must a correction talk make plain?
reviewCards.back: Name the act or result behind the concern, then name the expected change. Rank without specifics may win silence without repair.

reviewCards.front: Why can a consequence belong in serious feedback?
reviewCards.back: It shows that the gap carries stakes. Without it, the person may hear ordinary advice instead of a serious requirement.

reviewCards.front: What happens when a weak hiring call is repaired late?
reviewCards.back: The cost moves into team output, supervisory time, and later correction. Careful selection takes less effort than a late fix.

reviewCards.front: How does preparation reduce interview bias?
reviewCards.back: Predetermined requirements and task-focused questions keep attention on evidence. Improvising can overweight mood, liking, or recency.

implementationPlan.title: Write Evidence Before The Talk
implementationPlan.coreSkill: The skill is to write the demand before the conversation starts. In an interview, that means role requirement, past act, and job problem. In correction, it means gap, proof, expected change, and consequence.

ifThenPlans.plan: If the role demand is unwritten, then write it before the first interview question.
If the answer stays abstract, then ask for one past act or one job problem.
If the concern is serious, then name the behavior, change, and consequence before you speak.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before the moment arrives, spend 10 minutes: cross-out the vague opener and draft the exact line naming the evidence and the change.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Measure one number from the past week: how many hiring or correction notes start with the demand and evidence before the decision line.

memorableLines.text: Write the demand before the question.
memorableLines.why: It is the chapter's short command for interview preparation.

memorableLines.text: The interview does not reveal fit; the requirement reveals which answers count.
memorableLines.why: It reverses the reader's trust in a smooth exchange.

memorableLines.text: Evidence is the path from a claim to a visible act.
memorableLines.why: It defines evidence in the terms the chapter uses.
